columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: Focused on independent creators who want to be their own publishers and run subscription communities.
Free version available to start; platform fees / revenue share details vary (Locals is part of Rumble’s ecosystem in some reports).

strengths.title: All-in-one for creator communities
strengths.detail: Content publishing, discussions, events, memberships, and digital subscriptions in one platform.

strengths.title: Subscription-based revenue model
strengths.detail: Creators set tier prices; supporters pay for exclusive content and community access, recurring revenue.

strengths.title: Community and content tools
strengths.detail: Discussions/forums, groups, events, member directory, moderation, social feed, blogs, and media library.

strengths.title: Strong focus on creator independence
strengths.detail: Emphasizes that creators should be their own publishers, less sole reliance on big social platforms.

weaknesses.title: Smaller user base vs Patreon/OnlyFans
weaknesses.detail: Less widely known; creators often work harder to bring audience than on more established membership brands.

weaknesses.title: Platform and ecosystem lock-in
weaknesses.detail: Communities live inside Locals; portability of subscribers and content elsewhere can be challenging.

weaknesses.title: Potential reputational / political skew
weaknesses.detail: Strong adoption among certain political and commentary creators, association may affect brand perception for some audiences.

weaknesses.title: Less transparent fee structure
weaknesses.detail: Fee tables are less prominent than Patreon or Memberful; creators must dig into docs to understand full costs.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Locals is creator memberships with community features, subscriptions and exclusive content. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Locals makes it simple for creators to start a subscription-based community and make money directly from their supporters. Official site.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Locals side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Locals you can use Memberships and Community & Messaging as first-class product jobs. Fans already live on that membership surface and prefer tiers, posts, or patronage-native extras.

Using Kahana with Locals

You can use both. Locals keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep patronage-native fans on Locals. Dual-list related work on Kahana so people who browse libraries can find it, join a Club, and pay there too without rebuilding your whole fan stack.
